strengths: Addresses a clear and practical limitation of prior tool-creation methods (reliance on LLM internal knowledge) by grounding tool synthesis in structured external reference materials (textbooks), which is a sensible and useful idea.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct domains (causality, physics, chemistry) and four different LLM backbones (Llama-3.1-70B, Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT-4, GPT-4o), with consistent improvements over general-reasoning baselines, RAG baselines, general tool-creation methods (Creator), and domain-specific reasoning methods (Physics Reasoner, StructChem, ChemAgent).

Well-designed ablation study isolating the contributions of code-form tools vs. raw text (PoT+Hierarchical RAG) and hierarchical selection vs. similarity-based retrieval (REFTOOL sim), providing evidence that both components matter.
Human evaluation of tool quality (faithfulness, correctness, usefulness) and of consistency between LLM and human tool/chapter selection adds credibility beyond automated metrics alone.
Cost analysis showing REFTOOL is substantially cheaper and faster than comparable iterative/domain-specific methods (e.g., ChemAgent, Physics Reasoner) is a meaningful practical contribution.
Reasonable robustness checks: alternate tool-creation LLM (Gemini), reasoning model (o1-mini), and an additional unseen dataset (SciBench-fund) to test generalization/reusability of created tools.
Clear presentation with illustrative figures, case studies, and detailed prompts/appendix for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The performance gains, while consistent, are often modest and inconsistent across models/domains (e.g., in Chemistry, ChemAgent nearly matches or is close to REFTOOL for some models; in Physics, GPT-4 with PoT+REFTOOL barely beats PoT alone: 49.1 vs 45.6, and REFTOOL sometimes underperforms RAG or Creator on individual backbones, e.g., Llama-3.1-70B in Physics RAG 44.7 vs REFTOOL 53.5 is better but GPT-4 causality PoT+REFTOOL 38.7 is worse than ReAct+RAG 48.0), raising questions about the robustness/generality of the 11.3% average improvement claim, which appears sensitive to which baselines/models are aggregated.

The method fundamentally depends on the existence of a single well-matched, well-structured reference book per domain; the paper does not explore scenarios with multiple/overlapping/lower-quality references, conflicting reference sources, or domains lacking a clean hierarchical textbook, limiting the generality of the claimed framework beyond curated benchmark domains.

Reliance on GPT-4o (or Gemini) for tool creation contradicts the framing that REFTOOL overcomes 'the model's internal knowledge scope' — the tool-creation LLM must still correctly parse and interpret the reference material, so the approach does not fully escape the underlying model's comprehension limits (as acknowledged in the Limitations section, but not deeply investigated quantitatively, e.g., by measuring correlation between tool-creation model's domain competence and quality of resulting tools).

Benchmark scale is relatively small (114–269 questions per domain, and even smaller sub-datasets for chemistry, e.g., 118 total across three sub-datasets), which combined with the fairly small differences between methods raises concerns about statistical significance; no significance testing or variance/multiple-run analysis is reported.

The tool-creation process requires manually curating an appropriate, licensed textbook per domain and converting to LaTeX with preserved hierarchical structure — this human/engineering effort before running REFTOOL is nontrivial and somewhat downplays the 'human-free' framing claimed in the introduction.

The hierarchical tool selection mechanism (chapter then tool selection) is relatively simple (LLM prompted to pick from table of contents), and its comparison against a single alternative (embedding similarity retrieval) is somewhat narrow; other stronger baselines for hierarchical or agentic retrieval (e.g., iterative refinement, cross-encoder reranking) are not explored.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (LLM-based code tool synthesis, execution-based validation/refinement, hierarchical retrieval) are each individually well-established in prior tool-creation and RAG literature; the main contribution is combining them with reference grounding, which, while useful, is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The chemistry-domain human evaluation shows lower tool quality (89% example correctness) attributed to the LLM misunderstanding nuanced domain concepts, which is a red flag for scalability of the approach to more advanced or less textbook-friendly domains, but this issue is not explored further or mitigated.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated limitation of prior tool-creation methods (reliance on LLM's own possibly incomplete knowledge) by grounding tool creation in external reference materials such as textbooks.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental setup spanning three domains (causality, physics, chemistry) and four LLMs (Llama-3.1-70B, Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT-4, GPT-4o), with comparisons against general reasoning baselines, RAG variants, general-purpose tool creation (Creator), and domain-specific methods (Physics Reasoner, StructChem, ChemAgent).
Includes useful ablations isolating the effect of code-form tools vs. raw-text retrieval and hierarchical vs. similarity-based tool selection, which helps substantiate the design choices.

Provides a human evaluation of tool quality (faithfulness, correctness, usefulness) and of the consistency between LLM and human tool/chapter selection, adding some qualitative validation beyond pure accuracy numbers.
Reports cost/time analysis showing the method is considerably cheaper than iterative domain-specific baselines like Physics Reasoner and ChemAgent.

Reasonably transparent methodology with full prompts, implementation details, and additional robustness checks (alternate tool-creation LLM, reasoning model o1-mini, an additional physics dataset) provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Benchmarks used are quite small (114–269 questions per domain), and no statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported ~11.3% average improvement is robust rather than noise, especially given per-model/per-domain inconsistency (e.g., in Table 2 some REFTOOL variants barely beat or even trail RAG/PoT baselines for certain models).

The core idea combines several existing components (retrieval/RAG over structured documents, LLM-based tool synthesis, hierarchical retrieval) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique; the novelty is primarily in the specific combination and application to reference-grounded tool creation.

Reference materials (specific textbooks) are manually hand-picked by the authors per domain, and the framework assumes reference material with a clean hierarchical chapter/section structure (requiring conversion to LaTeX); this limits generalizability to domains lacking such structured, hierarchical references and raises reproducibility/practicality concerns (e.g., licensing/availability of textbooks, manual LaTeX conversion effort not fully detailed).

Improvements over the strongest domain-specific baseline are often marginal (e.g., chemistry: ChemAgent 56.3 vs. PoT+REFTOOL 57.7 average; physics sub-dataset SciBench-fund: REFTOOL ties rather than exceeds 4-shot Physics Reasoner), undercutting the claim of clear superiority.

Ablation studies (Table 4) are only conducted on two of the three domains (causality and physics) "due to computational constraints," leaving the chemistry domain's component-wise contribution unverified.
Human evaluation of tool quality and selection consistency is based on very small samples (20 tools/questions per domain), limiting the statistical reliability of these qualitative claims.

The method's dependence on the base LLM's ability to correctly parse and utilize reference content means it may inherit failure modes when the domain content is complex or nuanced (as acknowledged for chemistry), yet this limitation is not deeply analyzed with quantitative failure-mode breakdowns beyond a couple of case studies.

Comparisons to more recent/stronger tool-augmented or agentic methods, or a broader range of state-of-the-art LLMs, are limited; only one small-scale experiment with a reasoning model (o1-mini) is provided.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: existing self-generated tool creation methods rely on internal LLM knowledge and fail on specialized/novel domains, while REFTOOL grounds tool creation in external references (textbooks, grammar rules) to overcome this limitation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three knowledge-intensive scientific domains (causality, physics, chemistry) and four base LLMs, with comparisons against a wide range of relevant baselines (general reasoning, RAG, general-purpose tool creation, and domain-specific reasoning methods).

Strong and informative ablation studies isolating the contribution of code-form tools versus raw text (Hierarchical RAG) and hierarchical selection versus similarity-based retrieval, which convincingly support the two main design choices.

Thorough auxiliary analyses: cost/efficiency comparison showing large savings in time and API cost relative to methods like ChemAgent and Physics Reasoner, human evaluation of tool quality (faithfulness, correctness, usefulness), and human-vs-model tool-selection consistency analysis.

Good robustness checks: performance holds when using different LLMs for tool creation (Gemini, Llama), when applied to a reasoning model (o1-mini), and when tools are reused across a different dataset (SciBench-fund) in the same domain, supporting claims of dataset-agnostic reusability.

Demonstrated generalizability beyond scientific QA to a non-scientific, unstructured-reference setting (extremely low-resource Zhuang-Chinese translation), which strengthens the paper's broader claims.

Comparison against continued pretraining/fine-tuning on the same reference material provides useful evidence that RefTool's approach is more effective and portable across models than baking knowledge into weights.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing ideas (RAG-style retrieval, code-tool generation, hierarchical taxonomy construction) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is incremental relative to prior tool-creation and RAG literature.

Accuracy gains, while consistent, are often modest (a few points) and some baselines (e.g., ChemAgent, PoT+RAG) are competitive or occasionally superior on individual sub-datasets/models, raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement outside aggregated averages.

Several key evaluations rely on small sample sizes (e.g., 50 tools per domain for human evaluation, 20 questions per domain for tool-selection consistency, 71 questions for SciBench-fund), limiting the statistical robustness of some claims.

The method depends on manually curated reference materials appropriate to each benchmark's domain; this human curation step somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of the pipeline as fully "human-free" and automatic, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to the choice/quality of reference material.

The two-level (chapter/section) hierarchy is a simple design that may not scale well to very large or less well-structured knowledge bases, and the paper does not explore deeper hierarchies, overlapping topics, or tool-set growth/interference issues at larger scale.

Baseline/backbone LLMs used (GPT-4, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Llama-3.1-70B) are not state-of-the-art at the time of review; it is unclear whether the reported gains persist with more capable current models that may already possess stronger built-in domain knowledge, potentially shrinking REFTOOL's advantage.

Limited discussion of failure cases or error analysis of REFTOOL itself (e.g., when hierarchical tool selection picks the wrong tool, or when created tools are subtly incorrect despite passing validation on a single demonstration example), which would help characterize the method's robustness boundaries.
